title: Checkpoint: Islam
objective: After this level you can explain what Muslims believe, how they worship and how Islam's branches and law took shape.
summary: From the first revelation in 610 to the hadith collections of the 800s: how Muslim belief, worship, branches and law fit together.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 finale: from a mountain cave to the law schools.
cards.body: A revelation, a migration, a way of worship, a dispute over leadership and a body of law. Let's put Islam's story in order, then see how its parts fit.

events.label: First revelation on Mount Hira, Muslims believe
The hijra to Medina: Year 1 of the Islamic calendar
Muhammad dies; the leadership question begins
Death of al-Bukhari, compiler of "The Authentic"

cards.headline: Belief, practice, law
cards.body: Each part rests on the one before. Tawhid, the oneness of God, is put into words by the shahada, the first of the Five Pillars. The pillars then set a Muslim's day, year and lifetime, and the year's two great festivals follow the fast and the hajj: Eid al-Fitr ends Ramadan, and Eid al-Adha begins at the height of the hajj. Law grows from the same roots: the Quran first, then the hadith, a source for Islamic law, ritual and creed alike. Sunnis and Shia share this frame and differ over leadership.

cards.headline: Chapter 4 complete
learned: How Muslims understand Muhammad, the revelation of 610 and the hijra that starts their calendar.
What tawhid and the six articles of faith mean, and how the Five Pillars shape a Muslim's time.
How Muslims pray, fast and make the hajj, and why pilgrims dress alike.
Why Sunnis and Shia divided after 632, and how scholars build Islamic law from the Quran and hadith.

questions.prompt: Which order is right for these events in Muhammad's life?

options.label: First revelation, hijra, death in Medina
Hijra, first revelation, death in Medina
options.rationale: The revelation (610) came before the hijra (622).

options.label: First revelation, death in Medina, hijra
options.rationale: The hijra (622) came before his death (632).

options.label: Hijra, death in Medina, first revelation

questions.prompt: Muslim families sacrifice an animal and share the meat at the festival of _____.

options.label: Eid al-Fitr
options.rationale: Eid al-Fitr ends the Ramadan fast.

options.label: Laylat al-Qadr
options.rationale: That's the Night of Power in Ramadan.

options.label: Eid al-Adha
Ashura
options.rationale: Ashura is when Shia Muslims mourn Husayn.

questions.explanation: Eid al-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, remembers Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son.

questions.prompt: How does the shahada link Muslim belief to Muslim practice?

options.label: It lists the six articles of faith in order
options.rationale: It is a short testimony, not a list.

options.label: It states God's oneness and is the first pillar
It sets the times of the five daily prayers
options.rationale: The prayer times are a separate matter.

options.label: It records the Prophet's sayings for jurists

questions.explanation: The shahada voices tawhid, "There is no god but God", and it is the first of the Five Pillars.

questions.prompt: A new question arises that the Quran does not address. How would a jurist work toward a ruling?

options.label: By asking the ruler of the day to decide
options.rationale: Rulings come from the four sources, not a ruler.

options.label: By treating any personal opinion as sharia
options.rationale: Fiqh is careful human reasoning, never simply opinion.

options.label: By turning to the Sunnah, then consensus or analogy
By copying another religion's law
options.rationale: The four sources are the Quran, Sunnah, ijma and qiyas.

questions.explanation: Jurists work from the Quran, the Sunnah, ijma (consensus) and qiyas (analogy).

questions.prompt: Which Chapter 1 idea does the story of Sunnis and Shia illustrate best?

options.label: Every tradition is a family of subtraditions
Religion is belief in spiritual beings
options.rationale: That's Tylor's definition, not about branches.

options.label: Rites of passage have three stages
options.rationale: That's van Gennep's idea about rituals.

options.label: Scripture begins as oral tradition
options.rationale: True of the Quran, but not about the two branches.

questions.explanation: Sunnis and Shia share the Quran and the fundamentals but differ over leadership: one tradition, many subtraditions.
